query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr without sacrificing its strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance can be achieved by introducing a small amount of a low-density, low-melting-point element, such as aluminum, into the alloy composition.
generation.intervention: introduction of a small amount of aluminum
generation.conditions: room temperature and high temperature (up to 1000 °C)
generation.mechanism: aluminum addition reduces density while maintaining mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: reduced density without sacrificing mechanical performance
generation.boundary: room temperature and high temperature (up to 1000 °C)
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of aluminum to be added and the potential effects on corrosion resistance and other properties
generation.falsification_experiment: measure the density and mechanical properties of the alloy with and without aluminum addition, and compare the results to the baseline as-cast HfMoTaTiZr

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
We developed high-temperature high-damping high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties via Snoek relaxation.
